lessons.title: Identifying risks in animal management
lessons.html:
What is risk?

A hazard is anything that can cause harm: an aggressive bull, a broken crush, a dip chemical, a sick animal that carries a disease people can catch. Risk is how likely it is that the hazard will cause harm, and how serious that harm would be. Managing risk means finding the hazards, judging the risk and putting controls in place before anyone or any animal is hurt.

Types of risk on a livestock farm

AreaExamples
People safetyKicks, crushing, gorings, falls, needle-stick injuries, chemical splashes
Animal health and welfareDisease outbreaks, injuries in handling facilities, poisoning, starvation in drought
ZoonosesDiseases passed from animals to people, such as anthrax, brucellosis, rabies and tuberculosis
FinancialStock theft, losses from disease, poor fertility, market changes
EnvironmentOvergrazing, erosion, pollution of water by dips and manure

Legal duties

The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 requires the employer to identify hazards, assess risks and provide training and protective equipment; workers must follow safe procedures and report hazards. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 protects animal welfare, and the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 deals with controlled and notifiable diseases. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 deals with protecting veld, soil and water.

Doing a risk assessment

  1. Walk through each task, for example dipping, dosing, loading or calving.
  2. List the hazards at each step.
  3. Rate each risk as low, medium or high by likelihood and severity.
  4. Decide on controls and who is responsible.
  5. Review after any incident or change.

lessons.title: Controlling risks: people, animals and facilities
lessons.html:
The order of controls

Use the strongest control that is practical. First try to remove the hazard (for example cull a dangerous bull). Then engineer it out (a proper crush, non-slip floors, solid gates). Then use procedures and training. Last of all, use personal protective equipment (PPE) such as gloves, overalls, boots, face shields and respirators.

Handling facilities

  • Inspect crushes, races, loading ramps, gates and fences regularly and repair damage immediately.
  • Curved races and solid sides reduce baulking and stress.
  • Provide escape gaps or man-gates for handlers.

Safe handling practices

  • Use low-stress handling: work the flight zone, keep noise down, no beating.
  • Never work alone with bulls, boars, stallions or cows with newborn calves.
  • Assign tasks clearly and use agreed signals.
  • Take extra care with tired workers late in the day.

Chemicals and veterinary medicines

  • Use only registered products, and follow the label for dose, PPE and withdrawal period. Act 36 of 1947 governs stock remedies; follow the product label and your vet.
  • Store medicines and dips locked, away from feed, children and water sources.
  • Dispose of needles in a sharps container and empty containers as the label directs. Never reuse dip or chemical containers for water or food.
  • Record every treatment: animal, product, dose, date, withdrawal end date, person.

Zoonoses

Wear gloves when handling aborted foetuses, afterbirths and sick animals. Never open the carcass of an animal that died suddenly, because anthrax is possible; report it to the state vet. Keep dogs vaccinated against rabies and report animals behaving strangely.

lessons.title: Biosecurity, emergencies and record keeping
lessons.html:
Biosecurity

Biosecurity keeps diseases out of the herd and stops them spreading inside the farm.

  • Buy animals from known sources with health records.
  • Quarantine new arrivals in a separate camp before mixing them with the herd, for the period your vet advises.
  • Control visitors and vehicles; use foot baths and clean boots where needed.
  • Maintain boundary fences to keep out neighbours' stock and stray animals.
  • Follow a vaccination and parasite control programme drawn up with your vet.
  • Dispose of carcasses properly and quickly.
  • Report suspected controlled or notifiable diseases to the state veterinarian as required under the Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984.

Emergency planning

A supervisor must make sure the team knows what to do when things go wrong.

  • Display emergency numbers: ambulance, nearest clinic, vet, state vet, police for stock theft, fire services or fire protection association.
  • Keep a stocked first aid box and have trained first aiders. First aid must be learned through hands-on training with an accredited provider.
  • Plan for veld fires, floods and drought: fire breaks, evacuation of animals, emergency feed and water.
  • Report and investigate every incident and near-miss so that causes are fixed.

Records that reduce risk

  • Animal identification and stock counts (helps detect theft early).
  • Treatment and vaccination register.
  • Movement records and purchase documents.
  • Incident and injury register.
  • Equipment inspection checklists.

Regular counting of animals in each camp, checking brands and marks, and quick reporting to the police help reduce stock theft losses.

Key points

  • Identify hazards, assess risk and apply controls for every animal task.
  • Use the order of controls: remove, engineer, procedures, then PPE.
  • Follow labels and your vet for medicines and dips, and record every treatment.
  • Protect people from zoonoses and never open a carcass after sudden death.
  • Practise biosecurity, plan for emergencies and keep good records.

quiz.question: What is the difference between a hazard and a risk?

options.text: They mean exactly the same thing
A hazard can cause harm; risk is how likely and how serious that harm is
A risk is always a chemical; a hazard is always an animal

quiz.question: Which control is the LAST choice in the order of controls?

options.text: Engineering controls such as a proper crush

quiz.question: A steer has died suddenly in the veld. What should you do?

options.text: Open the carcass to find the cause
Feed the carcass to the dogs
Do not open it and report it to the state vet, as anthrax is possible

quiz.question: Why should new animals be quarantined?

options.text: To stop them bringing disease into the herd
To keep them away from water

quiz.question: Which law requires employers to identify hazards and provide training and protective equipment?

options.text: Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993
Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983

quiz.question: Empty dip containers may be rinsed and reused for drinking water.
Regular stock counts and checking brands help detect stock theft early.
Which details should be recorded for every animal treatment? (select all that apply)

options.text: The weather forecast for next week
The price of beef that day
